title: How To Avoid A Bad Start To Your School Year https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2013/08/17/how-to-avoid-a-bad-start-to-your-school-year/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin warns that the honeymoon period of a new school year can lull even vigilant teachers into complacency as small sloppiness creeps into routines around the third week. He describes how minor infractions—talking before being called on, slower compliance, murmuring during lessons—snowball if teachers merely remind, warn, or repeat themselves instead of addressing the root pattern. His central strategy is to 'never move on' until students are meeting the standard exactly as taught, pausing or restarting a routine from the beginning whenever necessary. He argues this proactive, detail-oriented stance—used consistently from day one—ultimately requires less intervention over time and produces sharper, more confident classroom behavior.
points: The excitement of a new year can mask a 'natural phenomenon' of gradual behavioral slippage that typically emerges around the third week of school.
Reminding, warning, and repeating are ineffective once minor slippage has taken hold, because students are already 'too far gone.'
The core strategy: never transition, start a lesson, or continue an activity until students are meeting the exact standard set for them.
Correcting slippage usually requires only a pause; other times it requires stopping, rewinding to the beginning, and starting the routine again.
Refusing to move forward until standards are met yields maximum time-on-task, confidence, and staggering long-term progress.
quotes: But just below the surface there is a danger lurking, a danger that can lullaby even the most vigilant teachers to sleep at the wheel.
If you look close, lo about the third week of school, you’ll notice a smidgen of sloppiness in the way your students line up for lunch or turn in their homework or gather themselves into groups.

And so they'll remind. They'll warn and threaten. They'll harp and harangue on the importance of listening, performing routines, and giving a good effort. But for the most part, it falls on deaf ears.
The strategy is this: Never move on until you’re getting exactly what you want from your students.
Usually, this takes nothing more than a pause. Other times, though, you may have to stop them in their tracks, rewind to the beginning, and start again.
When you steadfastly refuse to continue on and on, unsatisfied and unhappy with what you’re seeing in your students, there is no telling what can be accomplished.
